Algebra I · Lesson 8.1

The Basics of Inequality

Solve this lesson →All lessons

An inequality says one quantity is larger than another rather than equal to it. Nearly every move chapter 4 used on equations, adding the same number to both sides or scaling both sides, carries over unchanged. Exactly one does not, and finding which one, and why it fails, is the work of this lesson.

Problem
Three warehouses each store a whole number of pallets. Warehouse A stores more than warehouse B, and warehouse B stores more than warehouse C. Warehouse C stores 4747 pallets. Enter the smallest number of pallets warehouse A could store.
Show a hint
  • Comparing AA with CC in one step gives a true statement, but a weaker one than the two given comparisons allow. Work out what BB must be first.
  • BB is a whole number above 4747, so the smallest BB can be is 4848. Now take the same step one more time, from BB to AA.
Show the full solution
Since B>47B>47 and BB is a whole number, BB is at least 4848, and since A>BA>B, AA is at least 4949. The triple 49,48,4749,48,47 satisfies every condition, so the smallest count is 4949​. Comparing AA with CC directly gives the weaker A>47A>47, which is true but allows A=48A=48, a value the step through BB rules out.
Problem
At the start of a shift the first bin holds 415415 bolts and the second holds 392392. A machine then drops 168168 bolts into each bin. Enter how many more bolts the first bin holds than the second after the drop.
Show a hint
  • Ask what happens to the gap between the two bins, not to either count on its own.
  • The two counts become 415+168415+168 and 392+168392+168. Subtract one from the other.
Show the full solution
After the drop the counts are 415+168=583415+168=583 and 392+168=560392+168=560, and 583−560=23583−560=23​, the same gap as 415−392415−392 before it. Both counts go up by the same 168168, so the gap is untouched. Adding 168168 to the gap instead gives 191191, which would be right only if the bolts all went into the first bin.
Key idea
The statement a>ba>b means that a−ba−b is positive, and a≥ba≥b means that a−ba−b is positive or zero. Every rule in this chapter comes from reading a comparison that way. Transitivity. If a>ba>b and b>cb>c, then a−ba−b and b−cb−c are both positive, so their sum (a−b)+(b−c)=a−c(a−b)+(b−c)=a−c is positive as well, and a>ca>c. Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides leaves the direction alone, since (a+c)−(b+c)=a−b(a+c)−(b+c)=a−b is the difference it was before, which is why adding 168168 bolts to each bin left the gap at 2323.
Problem
A hiking club logged two trips. The first covered more than 3434 kilometers and the second covered more than 5757 kilometers, and neither distance has to be a whole number. Enter the largest number of kilometers that the two trips together are guaranteed to exceed.
Show a hint
  • Each trip has its own number to beat. The two comparisons point the same way, so they can be combined into one comparison about the total.
  • Write each trip as a comparison, then add the two left sides together and the two right sides together. Test the result on a sample pair such as 34.234.2 and 57.357.3.
Show the full solution
The first distance is more than 3434 and the second is more than 5757, and two comparisons pointing the same way may be added, so the total is more than 34+57=9134+57=91​. Writing the two distances as ff and ss, both f−34f−34 and s−57s−57 are positive, so (f+s)−91(f+s)−91 is positive as well. Distances just above 3434 and 5757 give a total just above 9191, so no larger number works.
Problem
A swim club beat a tennis club in wins two years running, 4141 to 1212 in the first year and 4444 to 3939 in the second. Subtracting the first comparison from the second, the way two equations are subtracted, gives the conclusion that the swim club's gain in wins was the larger one. Enter how many more wins the tennis club gained from the first year to the second than the swim club gained.
Show a hint
  • Both stated comparisons are true, so if subtracting one from the other were a legal move, its conclusion would have to be true as well. Work out each club's gain on its own.
  • The swim club went from 4141 to 4444 and the tennis club went from 1212 to 3939. Subtract within each club, then compare the two gains.
Show the full solution
The swim club gained 44−41=344−41=3 wins and the tennis club gained 39−12=2739−12=27, so the tennis club's gain is larger by 27−3=2427−3=24​. The subtraction gives 3>273>27, which is false even though both starting comparisons are true, so one inequality may not be subtracted from another.
Key idea
Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added. If x>yx>y and a>ba>b, then x−yx−y and a−ba−b are both positive, so their sum (x+a)−(y+b)(x+a)−(y+b) is positive and x+a>y+bx+a>y+b. They may not be subtracted. Subtracting them would need (x−a)−(y−b)=(x−y)−(a−b)(x−a)−(y−b)=(x−y)−(a−b) to be positive, and one positive number minus another is positive, zero or negative depending on which of the two is larger. With the swim club's gain of 33 and the tennis club's 2727, that difference is negative and the claim 3>273>27 is false.

Adding shifts both sides by the same amount and leaves the difference alone. Multiplying does not, since cx−cy=c(x−y)cx−cy=c(x−y) scales that difference by cc. Scaling a positive number by a positive cc keeps it positive, and scaling by a negative cc makes it negative, so multiplying splits into two cases. The next two problems take one of each.

Problem
A press stamped tt parts on Monday, with t>185t>185. On Tuesday it stamped 33 times Monday's number and then 4040 more. Apply those same two operations to both sides of t>185t>185. The result says Tuesday's count is greater than a certain number. Enter that number.
Show a hint
  • Tuesday's count is 3t+403t+40. Build it up from t>185t>185 one operation at a time.
  • Multiplying both sides by 33 is multiplying by a positive number, so the direction holds. Now add 4040 to both sides.
Show the full solution
Multiplying t>185t>185 by the positive number 33 keeps the direction, giving 3t>5553t>555, and adding 4040 to both sides keeps it as well, so Tuesday's count satisfies 3t+40>5953t+40>595​. The direction holds through both steps because 33 is positive and adding 4040 changes both sides by the same amount.
Problem
A student divides both sides of −7x>91−7x>91 by −7−7, leaves the inequality symbol pointing the same way, and concludes that the smallest integer xx can be is −12−12. Enter the largest integer xx can actually be.
Show a hint
  • Test the student's answer against the original statement before doing anything else. Put x=−12x=−12 into −7x−7x and compare the result with 9191.
  • Dividing both sides by −7−7 reverses the direction, so the allowed values sit below −13−13 rather than above it.
Show the full solution
Dividing −7x>91−7x>91 by −7−7 reverses the direction to x<−13x<−13, so the largest integer available is −14−14​. Checking, −7(−14)=98>91−7(−14)=98>91 while −7(−13)=91−7(−13)=91 is not above 9191. The student's −12−12 fails outright, since −7(−12)=84−7(−12)=84 sits below 9191.
Key idea
Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction. Start from x>yx>y, so x−yx−y is positive. For a negative cc, the product c(x−y)c(x−y) is a negative times a positive and so is negative, and since c(x−y)=cx−cyc(x−y)=cx−cy, that makes cx−cycx−cy negative and cx<cycx<cy. For a positive cc the same product stays positive, so cx>cycx>cy and the direction holds. Dividing by cc is multiplying by 1cc1​, which has the same sign as cc, so division splits the same two ways. Skipping that reversal in −7x>91−7x>91 produced the wrong −12−12.

Choosing between those two cases takes the sign of the multiplier. With a number written out the sign is there to read. With a letter it is not, and there are three cases rather than two, since multiplying by zero gives 00 on both sides. The next problem asks what that leaves.

Problem
It is given that a>ba>b, and kk is a real number whose sign is not stated. Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how kaka compares with kbkb.
Show a hint
  • Write ka−kb=k(a−b)ka−kb=k(a−b). Since a−ba−b is positive, the sign of ka−kbka−kb matches the sign of kk.
  • Fix a=9a=9 and b=2b=2, then try k=4k=4, k=−4k=−4 and k=0k=0 in turn, comparing kaka with kbkb each time.
Show the full solution
Here ka−kb=k(a−b)ka−kb=k(a−b) and a−ba−b is positive, so the sign of that difference is the sign of kk. With a=9a=9 and b=2b=2, k=4k=4 gives 36>836>8, k=−4k=−4 gives −36<−8−36<−8, and k=0k=0 gives 0=00=0, so the comparison is unknownunknown​. All three cases are possible, so an inequality cannot be multiplied by a letter whose sign is not known.
Fun fact
Thomas Harriot wrote the signs << and >> in his own papers and published none of his mathematics. Both first appeared in print in 1631, ten years after he died, in a book other hands assembled from those papers.
Problem
It is given that m>nm>n, with nothing said about the signs of mm and nn, and tt is a real number. Statement 1 is m−9>n−9m−9>n−9. Statement 2 is −2m>−2n−2m>−2n. Statement 3 is m5>n55m​>5n​. Statement 4 is mt>ntmt>nt. Statement 5 is m+n>2nm+n>2n. Statement 6 is m−n>0m−n>0. Enter how many of the six must be true.
Show a hint
  • Each statement is one move applied to both sides of m>nm>n. Name the move first, then ask whether that move preserves the direction.
  • Statement 5 is m>nm>n with nn added to both sides, and statement 6 is what m>nm>n means written out. Check the other four against what each operation does to the direction.
Show the full solution
Statement 1 subtracts 99 from both sides, statement 3 divides by the positive number 55, statement 5 adds nn to both sides, and statement 6 restates m>nm>n, so those four hold. Statement 2 multiplies by −2−2 without reversing the direction and statement 4 multiplies by a letter whose sign is not stated, so the count is 44​. The signs of mm and nn never matter here. Only the sign of each multiplier does.
Key idea
Multiply or divide both sides by a letter only when you know the sign of that letter. With m>nm>n, the comparison between kmkm and knkn is decided by the sign of km−kn=k(m−n)km−kn=k(m−n), and since m−nm−n is positive that sign is the sign of kk. If kk is positive then km>knkm>kn, if kk is negative then km<knkm<kn, and if k=0k=0 then km=knkm=kn. Three cases and three different outcomes, so nothing is settled until the sign is known, which is why mt>ntmt>nt stayed out of the count. Dividing by a letter needs the same condition and also k≠0k=0.

A square is never negative, whatever real number is put into it. Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, so the two factors are the same number and have the same sign. A positive times a positive is positive, a negative times a negative is positive, and 0×00×0 is 00. So x2x2 is never negative, whatever real xx is.

Problem
For every real number xx, the quantity x2+82−18xx2+82−18x is equal to (x−9)2+1(x−9)2+1. How does x2+82x2+82 compare with 18x18x at every real xx? Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown.
Show a hint
  • Deciding which is larger is the same as deciding the sign of the difference x2+82−18xx2+82−18x, and the problem already gives that difference in a second form.
  • (x−9)2(x−9)2 is the square of a real number, so it is never negative. Add 11 and ask how small the whole thing can get.
Show the full solution
The difference x2+82−18xx2+82−18x equals (x−9)2+1(x−9)2+1, and the square of a real number is never negative, so that difference is at least 11 at every real xx. Since the difference is always positive, x2+82x2+82 is greatergreater​. Rearranging the two quantities is not enough on its own. You need x2≥0x2≥0, applied to x−9x−9.
Problem
Each of these four pairs has x>yx>y. Pair 1 is x=9x=9, y=4y=4. Pair 2 is x=−2x=−2, y=−5y=−5. Pair 3 is x=7x=7, y=−1y=−1. Pair 4 is x=−4x=−4, y=−8y=−8. Enter how many of the four pairs satisfy 1x<1yx1​<y1​.
Show a hint
  • Work out both reciprocals in each pair and compare them. A negative number has a negative reciprocal, and of two negative numbers the one further from zero is the smaller.
  • Watch for the pair where xx is positive and yy is negative. There 1xx1​ is positive while 1yy1​ is negative, and no positive number is less than a negative one.
Show the full solution
Pair 1 gives 19<1491​<41​, pair 2 gives −12<−15−21​<−51​ and pair 4 gives −14<−18−41​<−81​, while pair 3 gives 17>−171​>−1, so the count is 33​. The three that flip have xx and yy on the same side of zero, and pair 3 does not.
Key idea
The trivial inequality. x2≥0x2≥0 for every real xx, with equality only at x=0x=0, since a nonzero xx times itself is a positive times a positive or a negative times a negative, and either way the product is positive. The reciprocal rule. If x>yx>y and xx and yy share a sign, then 1x<1yx1​<y1​. Dividing x>yx>y by xyxy gives 1y>1xy1​>x1​, and xyxy is positive exactly because the two signs match. With xx and yy on opposite sides of zero xyxy is negative and that division reverses instead, which is pair 3 above.

Every rule in this lesson is one question about a sign. Adding or subtracting the same number never changes a direction. Multiplying or dividing changes it exactly when the multiplier is negative, and leaves it undetermined when the multiplier is a letter of unstated sign. The last two problems run several of these moves in one chain.

Problem
Two numbers satisfy p>11p>11 and q>−3q>−3, and nothing else is known about either one. Enter the smallest number that 4−6(p+q)4−6(p+q) must stay below.
Show a hint
  • Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added, so pin down what p+qp+q must exceed before touching anything else.
  • That gives p+q>8p+q>8. Multiplying both sides by −6−6 is multiplying by a negative, so settle the direction before adding 44.
Show the full solution
Adding p>11p>11 and q>−3q>−3 gives p+q>8p+q>8, multiplying by −6−6 reverses the direction to −6(p+q)<−48−6(p+q)<−48, and adding 44 to both sides gives 4−6(p+q)<−444−6(p+q)<−44​. Skipping the reversal would give 4−6(p+q)>−444−6(p+q)>−44, which is false at p=12p=12 and q=−2q=−2, since those give −56−56.
Problem
Two numbers satisfy 15−8s>15−8t15−8s>15−8t, and their product stst is positive. Neither one is known to be positive on its own. Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how 1tt1​ compares with 1ss1​.
Show a hint
  • Two moves. First turn 15−8s>15−8t15−8s>15−8t into a comparison between ss and tt alone, watching the step that reverses the direction.
  • That gives s<ts<t. The reciprocal rule needs the two numbers to share a sign, and st>0st>0 says exactly that even though neither sign is known on its own.
Show the full solution
Subtracting 1515 from both sides gives −8s>−8t−8s>−8t, and dividing by −8−8 reverses the direction to s<ts<t. Since st>0st>0 the two share a sign, so the reciprocal rule applies and 1tt1​ compared with 1ss1​ is lessless​. Both sign cases check out, s=1,t=2s=1,t=2 giving 12<121​<1 and s=−2,t=−1s=−2,t=−1 giving −1<−12−1<−21​. Drop st>0st>0 and the answer is unknown, since s=−1,t=2s=−1,t=2 gives 1t>1st1​>s1​.

Every rule here says what one move does to a comparison already in hand. Lesson 8.2, Which Is Bigger, uses them in the other direction. It starts with two specific quantities too awkward to compute outright and looks for the move that settles which one is larger.

Practice these ideas

Practice
ww is an integer and w−18>45w−18>45. Enter the smallest value ww can be.
Show the solution
Adding 1818 to both sides leaves the direction unchanged, giving w>63w>63, so the smallest integer available is 6464​. Checking, 64−18=46>4564−18=46>45 while 63−18=4563−18=45 is not above 4545.
Practice
Integers aa, bb, and cc satisfy a>ba>b and b>cb>c, with c=61c=61. Enter the smallest possible value of aa.
Show the solution
Since b>61b>61 and bb is an integer, bb is at least 6262, and a>ba>b makes aa at least 6363. The triple 63,62,6163,62,61 meets every condition, so the answer is 6363​. Chaining to a>61a>61 first is true but weaker, since a=62a=62 would need an integer bb with 61<b<6261<b<62, and there is none.
Practice
A number gg satisfies g>16g>16. Enter the largest number that 7g7g must exceed.
Show the solution
Multiplying g>16g>16 by the positive number 77 leaves the direction unchanged, so 7g>1127g>112​. Nothing larger works, since gg can sit just above 1616, which puts 7g7g just above 112112.
Practice
Real numbers mm and nn satisfy m>30m>30 and n>17n>17. Enter the largest number that m+nm+n must exceed.
Show the solution
Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added, so m+n>30+17=47m+n>30+17=47​. Nothing larger works, since taking mm and nn just above 3030 and 1717 makes m+nm+n as close to 4747 as we like.
Practice
qq is an integer and q8>138q​>13. Enter the smallest value qq can be.
Show the solution
Multiplying both sides by the positive number 88 keeps the direction, giving q>104q>104, so the smallest integer is 105105​. Checking, 1058=13.1258105​=13.125 is above 1313 while 1048=138104​=13 is not.
Practice
A number kk satisfies k>3k>3, and nothing else is known about it. Enter the smallest number that −8k−8k must stay below.
Show the solution
Multiplying k>3k>3 by −8−8 reverses the direction, so −8k<−24−8k<−24​. Keeping >> would give the false claim −8k>−24−8k>−24, since k=4k=4 gives −32−32, and −32−32 is not above −24−24.
Practice
nn is an integer and −5n>37−5n>37. Enter the largest value nn can be.
Show the solution
Dividing −5n>37−5n>37 by −5−5 reverses the direction to n<−7.4n<−7.4, so the largest integer is −8−8​. Checking, −5(−8)=40>37−5(−8)=40>37 while −5(−7)=35−5(−7)=35 is not above 3737.
Practice
Both 20>320>3 and b>1b>1 are true, and bb is an integer. Subtracting the second comparison from the first would claim 20−b>3−120−b>3−1. Enter the smallest integer bb that makes that claim false.
Show the solution
The claim reads 20−b>220−b>2, which holds only while b<18b<18. At b=18b=18 it reads 2>22>2, which is false, so the answer is 1818​. Both starting comparisons still hold at b=18b=18, so subtracting one comparison from another is not a legal move.
Practice
It is given that a>ba>b, and t=0t=0. Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how tata compares with tbtb.
Show the solution
With t=0t=0, both tata and tbtb are 00, so the two are equalequal​. Zero is neither positive nor negative, so neither multiplication rule applies, and the given a>ba>b makes no difference to the comparison.
Practice
It is given that u>vu>v. Statement 1 is u+3>v+3u+3>v+3. Statement 2 is 4u>4v4u>4v. Statement 3 is u−2>v−2−2u​>−2v​. Statement 4 is u−v>0u−v>0. Statement 5 is −u<−v−u<−v. Statement 6 is u+v>2vu+v>2v. Enter how many of the six must be true.
Show the solution
Dividing both sides by −2−2 reverses the direction, so statement 3 is the only one that fails and the count is 55​. Statements 1, 4 and 6 come from adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides, statement 2 from multiplying by the positive 44, and statement 5 from multiplying by −1−1 with the direction reversed.
Practice
It is given that x>yx>y. For how many of k=−3k=−3, k=0k=0 and k=5k=5 is kx>kykx>ky guaranteed? Enter that count.
Show the solution
The sign of kx−ky=k(x−y)kx−ky=k(x−y) is the sign of kk, since x−yx−y is positive. So k=5k=5 gives kx>kykx>ky, k=−3k=−3 gives kx<kykx<ky, and k=0k=0 gives kx=kykx=ky, leaving 11​. Three values of kk and three different outcomes, so you may only multiply both sides by a letter when you know its sign.
Practice
A real number cc satisfies c2≤0c2≤0. Enter the value of (c+5)(c+8)(c+5)(c+8).
Show the solution
Since c2≥0c2≥0 for every real cc, the condition c2≤0c2≤0 can hold only when c2=0c2=0, so c=0c=0 and (0+5)(0+8)=40(0+5)(0+8)=40​. The trivial inequality pins cc to a single value, so nothing else about cc has to be found.
Practice
For every real number xx, the quantity x2+121−22xx2+121−22x is equal to (x−11)2(x−11)2. Enter the value of x2+121x2+121 at the one real number xx where it equals 22x22x.
Show the solution
x2+121x2+121 equals 22x22x exactly when x2+121−22x=0x2+121−22x=0, which is (x−11)2=0(x−11)2=0, so x=11x=11. Then x2+121=121+121=242x2+121=121+121=242​, and 22(11)=24222(11)=242 agrees. A square is never negative, so (x−11)2(x−11)2 is 00 at one value of xx and positive everywhere else, which is why x2+121x2+121 is never below 22x22x.
Practice
The numbers x=15x=15 and y=6y=6 are both positive, and x>yx>y. Enter the value of 1y−1xy1​−x1​ as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
With a common denominator of 3030, 16−115=530−230=330=11061​−151​=305​−302​=303​=101​​. The reciprocal rule says that when x>yx>y and both are positive, 1x<1yx1​<y1​, so this difference had to come out positive.
Practice
The numbers x=10x=10 and y=−4y=−4 satisfy x>yx>y, so the reciprocal rule would claim 1x<1yx1​<y1​. Enter the value of 1x−1yx1​−y1​ as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
The reciprocals are 110101​ and −14−41​, so 110−(−14)=220+520=720101​−(−41​)=202​+205​=207​​. The difference is positive, which says 1x>1yx1​>y1​, the opposite of the claim. These two numbers sit on opposite sides of zero, and the rule needs them on the same side.
Practice
A number zz satisfies z<6z<6, and y=9−4zy=9−4z. Enter the largest number that yy must exceed.
Show the solution
Multiplying z<6z<6 by −4−4 reverses the direction to −4z>−24−4z>−24, and adding 99 to both sides gives 9−4z>−159−4z>−15​. Skipping the reversal gives y<−15y<−15 instead, which is false at z=0z=0, where y=9y=9.
Practice
An integer mm satisfies 1m<17m1​<71​ and m>0m>0. Enter the smallest value mm can be.
Show the solution
Both numbers are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the comparison and 1m<17m1​<71​ becomes m>7m>7, making the smallest integer 88​. Checking, 18<1781​<71​. The condition m>0m>0 matters, since m=−3m=−3 also satisfies 1m<17m1​<71​ but is not greater than 77.
